=== CALL C0398 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, can you hear me alright? I'm Gemma.
Tariq: Yeah, fine. Tariq. Hi.
Gemma: Hi Tariq. Erm, so, did you do that puzzle thing at the start? I was useless, I'm not gonna lie, I got about three and then sort of just stared at it.
Tariq: The pattern ones? Yeah. Some of the later ones were a bit ambiguous, I thought. Two of them had more than one defensible answer.
Gemma: Oh, that makes me feel better actually! I thought it was just me. So what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
Tariq: I run operations for a facilities management company. Office cleaning, security, maintenance, that kind of thing, across London. So about forty contracts, five site managers, and a lot of people ringing me when a lift breaks.
Gemma: Forty! Blimey. That sounds really stressful, is it?
Tariq: It can be. Had a client ring at nine o'clock last night about a lift. It's fine. Most of it's just catching problems before the client does. What about you?
Gemma: Erm, so, I'm a dog groomer, well, assistant dog groomer, two days a week in Walsall. So bathing, drying, nails, and I'm learning the proper cuts off my boss. And I'm doing a psychology degree with the Open University, which is sort of the main thing really, I want to go into mental health eventually. That's probably more than you asked, sorry!
Tariq: No, that's fine. Open University, part-time? Evenings?
Gemma: Yeah, evenings mostly. Second year.
Tariq: Respect for that, honestly. I did my CIMA part-time while I was working. Accountancy qualification. Took me years. It's the evenings that kill you, right, you come in knackered and then you've got to sit down and do another three hours.
Gemma: Yes! That's exactly it. And I've got a dog snoring on the settee downstairs which doesn't help, I can hear him from here. Did you, like, did you find it got easier?
Tariq: Not easier. You just get more disciplined about it. I blocked out the same nights every week and didn't move them. If you leave it to how you feel, you won't do it.
Gemma: Same nights every week. Yeah, that's probably where I'm going wrong, I sort of do it when there's a deadline, do you know what I mean?
Tariq: Everyone does. How are your marks?
Gemma: Erm, decent actually. Better than I thought. I always think I'm not clever enough for it and then the mark comes back and it's fine.
Tariq: Then you're clever enough for it. That's what the marks are for.
Gemma: Ha, that's fair. I'll tell myself that. Are you in London then, like, central?
Tariq: Gants Hill. Ilford. Live with my parents, actually, in the house I grew up in.
Gemma: Oh, me too! I moved back in with my mum and dad a couple of years ago. I'm always a bit embarrassed saying it, at thirty-five.
Tariq: I'm forty. Don't be embarrassed. Dad's getting older, someone's got to be there. My mum still thinks I work too much, mind.
Gemma: That's my dad! I worry about him, he won't go the doctor's for anything. Sunday dinner's my mum's thing though, that's sacred in our house.
Tariq: Sundays my sister comes round with her three kids. It's chaos. Good chaos.
Gemma: Aw. I've got two nieces, I do their hair for school plays and that. Do you do anything outside work, or is it all lifts and spreadsheets?
Tariq: Badminton on Wednesdays, cycling Saturdays. And I read a lot. History, mostly. Cities, architecture.
Gemma: Ooh, I do Zumba on Wednesdays! Not the same, is it.
Tariq: Not really, no.
Gemma: Ha! Fair. Is there a place you'd most like to... sorry, a place you've been that you'd sort of recommend?
Tariq: Samarkand. Uzbekistan. The Registan. If you ever get the chance, honestly, the tilework alone is worth the...

=== CALL C0399 ===
Nicola: Hello! Oh there you are. I'm Nicola, hiya.
Graham: Hello, duck, Graham. Can you hear me alright? I've got the volume up full here.
Nicola: Loud and clear! Where are you then?
Graham: Beeston, just outside Nottingham. You?
Nicola: Frome, in Somerset. Sort of near Bath, if that helps.
Graham: Oh, I know Frome. Went through it on the train once, years ago. Lovely little town, all them steep streets.
Nicola: Proper steep, yeah, my calves are ruined. So what do you do, Graham?
Graham: I'm a postie. Well, part-time, early shifts, walking round in Chilwell. Up at half four. I did nearly thirty years as a civil engineer before that, highways, drainage, project management, and then I sort of... decided I'd had enough of it, you know. So now I walk about twenty thousand steps a day and nobody rings me about culverts.
Nicola: Twenty thousand! That's amazing. I'm lucky if I do parkrun without walking half of it.
Graham: Do you do parkrun? I do Beeston. Careful pace, mind, I'm not breaking any records.
Nicola: Saturdays, when I can be bothered. I chat at the back with my mate. Does it count if you walk half of it, do you reckon?
Graham: No, see, it counts. It's five K, you got round. That's the whole point of it. Anyone who says otherwise wants a word with themselves.
Nicola: Ha, I'm telling my friend that. I'm a dental hygienist, by the way, two days a week at a practice in Frome.
Graham: Oh, right. I'll keep me mouth shut then. I'm terrible for flossing.
Nicola: Everyone says that! I never tell anyone off, honestly. Have you got a dog? I've got a Jack Russell, Biscuit, she won't go out if it's raining.
Graham: No dog of me own, but there's a springer on my round who waits at the gate every morning. I save him a treat. Not your Biscuit.
Nicola: Ha! Do you live on your own then?
Graham: I do, yeah. Separated a couple of years. I've got two grown-up kids, son in Nottingham who I see most Sundays, and me daughter's up in Leeds. Don't see her as much as I'd like.
Nicola: Mine's in Cardiff. Megan, she's twenty, at uni. And Alfie's fifteen, still at home, eats everything in the fridge.
Graham: Fifteen, oh, I remember that. We used to do a big shop and it'd be gone by Tuesday.
Nicola: Exactly that. What do you do with yourself then, apart from the round?
Graham: Oh, I keep busy. Watercolours at an evening class, pub quiz Tuesdays, I'm learning Italian on Duolingo, four hundred and something days. Did a rail trip round northern Italy last year, had it all on a spreadsheet, every train, every backup.
Nicola: A spreadsheet! I'd be hopeless, I just go wherever my friends have booked. I did Lisbon with the girls like that.
Graham: Lisbon's on the list. Is it as hilly as they say?
Nicola: Worse than Frome! But proper lovely. The custard tarts, you know? And everyone was so friendly.
Graham: That'll do me. And Forest are... well, we won't talk about Forest.
Nicola: I don't follow football really, I watch the rugby in the pub for the atmosphere.
Graham: Rugby. Oh dear. We'll have to agree to disagree there, duck.
Nicola: Ha! Fair enough. Do you paint the canals then? I bet you do.
Graham: How'd you guess? There's one behind me, actually, Beeston lock, it's a bit crooked on the wall, I keep meaning to...

=== CALL C0400 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Oh, it's you, I spotted your dog lead in your picture! I'm Gemma.
Nicola: Ha, Nicola! That's Biscuit's lead. She's in her bed just down there, you'll probably hear her snoring in a minute.
Gemma: Aw, we've got a snorer too, Duke, he's my mum and dad's Staffie. He's ancient. What's Biscuit?
Nicola: Jack Russell, and she's getting on as well, twelve now. Proper stubborn. She won't go out if it's raining, just plants her feet on the doorstep.
Gemma: Oh my God, I see that every week at work! I'm a dog groomer, well, assistant, and we've got this cockapoo who absolutely hates the dryer. She sort of tries to climb up you, do you know what I mean?
Nicola: Ah no, bless her. A groomer, that's lovely. Do you get bitten much?
Gemma: Erm, not loads. You learn to read them. With the nervous ones you just go slow and talk to them, and most of them settle. It's the owners that are harder sometimes, when you've got to tell them the dog's matted to the skin and they don't want to hear it.
Nicola: That's my job exactly! I'm a dental hygienist. You've got to tell people their gums are bleeding without making them feel told off. Same thing really, isn't it? Just with less fur.
Gemma: Ha! Less fur. Yeah. Do you like it?
Nicola: I do, honestly. It's two days a week. I went part-time after my divorce so I could be around for the kids. Have you got kids? I thought you looked like a busy mum in your photo, sorry if that's wrong!
Gemma: No, no kids! That's my nieces in the picture. I'm a professional auntie. Erm, all my friends have got kids though, so I sort of get the busy mum bit second-hand.
Nicola: Being an auntie's the best bit anyway, you get to hand them back.
Gemma: That's what my mum says! How old are yours?
Nicola: Megan's twenty, she's at uni in Cardiff, and Alfie's fifteen. He's got his GCSEs next year so I'm trying not to nag. Failing, but trying.
Gemma: Is it weird with your daughter away?
Nicola: Erm, yeah, a bit. More than I let on, probably. The house is quieter. She rings when she wants money, ha.
Gemma: I'm doing a degree as well, actually, Open University, psychology. So I'm sort of a student too, just thirty-five and living with my mum and dad.
Nicola: Oh, good for you! Psychology, what do you want to do with it?
Gemma: Something in mental health, maybe counselling. I had counselling myself in my twenties and it really helped, so. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes, isn't it?
Nicola: No, not at all, that's a proper good reason to do it. You'd be brilliant, you're easy to talk to.
Gemma: Aw, thank you. What do you do for fun then?
Nicola: Gigs, mostly. There's a venue in Frome, the Cheese and Grain, and I'm going to a tribute night there in a couple of weeks. And swimming, and netball, the back-to-netball thing.
Gemma: I do Zumba! Wednesdays. It nearly killed me last week.
Nicola: Ha, I've seen those classes, they're no joke. Do you go with friends?
Gemma: Yeah, with my mate Kirsty. We mostly go so we can have a Greggs after and not feel guilty.
Nicola: That's the only reason to exercise, honestly. Did you do that puzzle at the start, by the way? I was hopeless.
Gemma: Me too! The bloke I just had said two of them had more than one right answer, so I'm blaming the puzzle.
Nicola: Ooh, I like that, we'll blame the—

=== CALL C0401 ===
Graham: Hello, Graham. You're Tariq, is it?
Tariq: That's right. Hi.
Graham: I was looking at your photo earlier, you've got a fair few history books there. What are you reading at the minute?
Tariq: Something on the London docks. How the whole system worked before containerisation. It's quite good, actually.
Graham: Oh, now you're talking. Industrial stuff's my thing. Canals mostly, the Erewash and the Beeston canal, round here. I was a civil engineer for nearly thirty year, so I'm always looking at the drainage and the lock gates rather than the pretty bits.
Tariq: Civil engineer. What sort of work?
Graham: Highways and drainage schemes, then project management towards the end, for a consultancy in Derby. Left at fifty-five. Now I'm a postie, part-time, walking round in Chilwell.
Tariq: That's quite a change.
Graham: It is, yeah. I'll be honest, it was a bad year, stress, and then the heart started doing funny things. So I wanted something with a start and a finish, you know. You go out, you deliver it, you come back, it's done.
Tariq: I get that. My job never finishes. I run operations for a facilities company in London, about forty contracts. Somebody's always got a problem.
Graham: Oh, I don't miss that. Mind, I still can't help meself. Last month I told me manager how the walks should be split up. Three of them are daft, there's lads crossing each other's routes twice a morning.
Tariq: Did he listen?
Graham: Did he heck.
Tariq: That's the problem, right. Most people don't want the fix, they just want to not be blamed. I do the scheduling for a few hundred cleaners and security staff, and the hardest part isn't the rota. It's getting the site managers to actually follow it.
Graham: No, see, I'd put it the other way. If they're not following it, half the time it's because whoever wrote it never walked the job. I was guilty of that meself.
Tariq: Fair point. Partly. Some of them just don't want to.
Graham: Ha, some of them, yeah. Do you get out of London much?
Tariq: One proper trip a year. Japan last time, Uzbekistan before that. I plan it on a spreadsheet, train times, everything.
Graham: A spreadsheet! Thank God, I thought it were just me. I did northern Italy last year by rail, every connection on its own tab, backup options in a different colour.
Tariq: Backup options in a different colour. That's the right way to do it.
Graham: Me daughter thinks I'm mad. I'm learning Italian an' all, four hundred and twelve days on Duolingo.
Tariq: That's commitment. I'm on an app for my written Urdu and I'm nowhere near four hundred days.
Graham: Get on with it then! You follow football? I'm a Forest man meself.
Tariq: No. Cricket. Pakistan, and Essex.
Graham: Cricket. Well, at least it's not rugby. I've just had a lady tell me she watches rugby.
Tariq: Pakistan will wind you up more than any football team, I promise you. They collapsed from a winning position last week. Again.
Graham: Ha, you want to try being Forest. We've had forty years of—

=== CALL C0402 ===
Gemma: Hiya! Graham, is it? I'm Gemma.
Graham: Hello, duck. Yes, Graham. Can you hear me alright?
Gemma: Yeah, perfect. I've got to say, when I saw your photo you reminded me of my dad. The canal painting and everything. He's always walking the canal.
Graham: Oh, I'll take that as a compliment, I think. Where are you?
Gemma: Walsall. I walk our dog along the canal most days, and round the Arboretum.
Graham: Walsall canal. Now that's a proper bit of history, that. All them branches round there used to be packed with boats for the foundries and the leather works.
Gemma: My dad worked in a leather factory! Then he drove a delivery van.
Graham: There you go. Me dad drove a lorry. And me mum was a dinner lady.
Gemma: No way, so was my mum! She's retired now, but the kids at the school still stop her in Asda.
Graham: Ha, mine were the same. Couldn't go anywhere. So what do you do, Gemma?
Gemma: Erm, I'm an assistant dog groomer, two days a week, and I'm doing a psychology degree with the Open University. Second year. I want to go into mental health, eventually, if I don't leave it too late.
Graham: Too late? How old are you, if you don't mind me asking?
Gemma: Thirty-five.
Graham: No, see, that's not late, that. I'm fifty-eight and I've just started watercolours and Italian. You've got thirty year of work in you yet. And I saw them course books in your picture. That's somebody who means it.
Gemma: Aw, that's really kind. I do worry I'm not clever enough sometimes. My marks are alright though.
Graham: Well then. Marks don't lie. What are you doing on it at the minute?
Gemma: Erm, a module on anxiety and how people cope with stress, which is sort of close to home, I had a bit of that in my twenties. Sorry, is that too much? I always say too much.
Graham: Not at all. I had a bad year meself before I packed in engineering. Stress, then me heart started going funny. So I know a bit about it from the wrong end. You'd be good at that job, I reckon. You're easy to talk to.
Gemma: That's two people who've said that today, I'm gonna get big-headed. Are you alright now, with your heart?
Graham: Oh, it's managed. Tablets, and I walk twenty thousand steps a day on the round. I'm a postie now. Get up at half four.
Gemma: Half four! I'd be useless. My dad won't even go the doctor's, he's terrible. I'm always on at him.
Graham: Keep on at him. Honestly. I left it far too long, I should've gone months before I did.
Gemma: I'll tell him a postman from Beeston said so. Do you follow football? My dad drags me to Walsall a couple of times a season.
Graham: Forest, all me life. Walsall, though, I'll give you credit for that, it takes a special kind of suffering.
Gemma: Ha! It does. We have a bacon bap at half time and that's the best bit.
Graham: A bap? It's a cob, duck.
Gemma: It's a bap! What's a cob?
Graham: It's a cob. Same thing, round, bread, bacon in it. Saturday morning, there's a new bakery on the High Road does a cracking—

=== CALL C0403 ===
Nicola: Hiya! Last one, isn't it? I'm Nicola.
Tariq: Tariq. Hi. Yeah, last one.
Nicola: How've you found it? I've had a lovely time, everyone's been so chatty.
Tariq: It's been fine. Better than I expected, honestly.
Nicola: Ha, what did you expect?
Tariq: Three minutes of talking about the weather. It's been more interesting than that.
Nicola: Well, I'll try not to mention the weather then. So what do you do, Tariq?
Tariq: Operations for a facilities management company in London. Cleaning, security, maintenance contracts for office buildings. You?
Nicola: I'm a dental hygienist, two days a week in Frome. In Somerset.
Tariq: Right. So you're the one who tells people off about flossing.
Nicola: No! I never tell anyone off. That's the whole trick, you chat them through it, you ask about their grandkids, and they don't even notice you're scraping away. It's sort of like being a hairdresser, only with more blood.
Tariq: That's a terrible selling point.
Nicola: Ha, yeah, don't put that on the leaflet. You drink a lot of coffee, I reckon. You've got the look.
Tariq: Sorry, what look is that exactly?
Nicola: I don't know, organised. Busy. Bit tired round the eyes. Sorry, that's rude!
Tariq: No, it's accurate. Three or four a day. I'm fussy about it, though, there's a new place by Stratford station that's actually decent.
Nicola: Well, I won't lecture you. Do you get away much, with a job like that?
Tariq: One proper trip a year. Japan was the last one. Before that Uzbekistan, Samarkand and Bukhara. And Andalusia, for the Alhambra.
Nicola: Oh, I've always wanted to see the Alhambra! I did Lisbon with my girlfriends. Was it worth it?
Tariq: Completely. Go early, book the Nasrid Palaces slot weeks ahead, and go to Córdoba as well, the Mezquita. People skip Córdoba and they shouldn't. It's about two hours on the train, there's a fast one from Granada now, and honestly the inside of the Mezquita, all those arches going on and on in the half-dark, it's one of the best buildings I've ever stood in.
Nicola: See, now I want to go. You'd be a proper good person to travel with, you'd know where everything was.
Tariq: I would. I'd also want to leave at seven in the morning.
Nicola: Ah, that's me out then. I'm more of a sit at the next table and make friends with the waiter sort of person. I'm going to New Zealand one day, that's my big one.
Tariq: One day meaning when?
Nicola: Erm, once Alfie's done his GCSEs and I've saved up. So, never, probably!
Tariq: Put a date on it. Then work back from the date. Otherwise it stays "one day".
Nicola: That's proper sensible. Annoyingly sensible. Do you do that with everything?
Tariq: Pretty much. My mum says I'd plan breakfast if she let me.
Nicola: Ha! I like your mum already. Has she got—

Nicola: I do, honestly. It's two days a week. I went part-time after my divorce so I could be around for the kids. Have you got kids? I thought you looked like a busy mum in your photo, sorry if that's wrong!
Gemma: No, no kids! That's my nieces in the picture. I'm a professional auntie. Erm, all my friends have got kids though, so I sort of get the busy mum bit second-hand.
Nicola: Being an auntie's the best bit anyway, you get to hand them back.
Gemma: That's what my mum says! How old are yours?
Nicola: Megan's twenty, she's at uni in Cardiff, and Alfie's fifteen. He's got his GCSEs next year so I'm trying not to nag. Failing, but trying.
Gemma: Is it weird with your daughter away?
Nicola: Erm, yeah, a bit. More than I let on, probably. The house is quieter. She rings when she wants money, ha.
Gemma: I'm doing a degree as well, actually, Open University, psychology. So I'm sort of a student too, just thirty-five and living with my mum and dad.
Nicola: Oh, good for you! Psychology, what do you want to do with it?
Gemma: Something in mental health, maybe counselling. I had counselling myself in my twenties and it really helped, so. Sorry, that's a bit heavy for three minutes, isn't it?
Nicola: No, not at all, that's a proper good reason to do it. You'd be brilliant, you're easy to talk to.
Gemma: Aw, thank you. What do you do for fun then?
Nicola: Gigs, mostly. There's a venue in Frome, the Cheese and Grain, and I'm going to a tribute night there in a couple of weeks. And swimming, and netball, the back-to-netball thing.
Gemma: I do Zumba! Wednesdays. It nearly killed me last week.
Nicola: Ha, I've seen those classes, they're no joke. Do you go with friends?
Gemma: Yeah, with my mate Kirsty. We mostly go so we can have a Greggs after and not feel guilty.
Nicola: That's the only reason to exercise, honestly. Did you do that puzzle at the start, by the way? I was hopeless.
Gemma: Me too! The bloke I just had said two of them had more than one right answer, so I'm blaming the puzzle.
Nicola: Ooh, I like that, we'll blame the—
calls.C0401:
Graham: Hello, Graham. You're Tariq, is it?
Tariq: That's right. Hi.
Graham: I was looking at your photo earlier, you've got a fair few history books there. What are you reading at the minute?
Tariq: Something on the London docks. How the whole system worked before containerisation. It's quite good, actually.
Graham: Oh, now you're talking. Industrial stuff's my thing. Canals mostly, the Erewash and the Beeston canal, round here. I was a civil engineer for nearly thirty year, so I'm always looking at the drainage and the lock gates rather than the pretty bits.
Tariq: Civil engineer. What sort of work?
Graham: Highways and drainage schemes, then project management towards the end, for a consultancy in Derby. Left at fifty-five. Now I'm a postie, part-time, walking round in Chilwell.
Tariq: That's quite a change.
Graham: It is, yeah. I'll be honest, it was a bad year, stress, and then the heart started doing funny things. So I wanted something with a start and a finish, you know. You go out, you deliver it, you come back, it's done.
Tariq: I get that. My job never finishes. I run operations for a facilities company in London, about forty contracts. Somebody's always got a problem.
Graham: Oh, I don't miss that. Mind, I still can't help meself. Last month I told me manager how the walks should be split up. Three of them are daft, there's lads crossing each other's routes twice a morning.
Tariq: Did he listen?
Graham: Did he heck.
Tariq: That's the problem, right. Most people don't want the fix, they just want to not be blamed. I do the scheduling for a few hundred cleaners and security staff, and the hardest part isn't the rota. It's getting the site managers to actually follow it.
Graham: No, see, I'd put it the other way. If they're not following it, half the time it's because whoever wrote it never walked the job. I was guilty of that meself.
Tariq: Fair point. Partly. Some of them just don't want to.
Graham: Ha, some of them, yeah. Do you get out of London much?
Tariq: One proper trip a year. Japan last time, Uzbekistan before that. I plan it on a spreadsheet, train times, everything.
Graham: A spreadsheet! Thank God, I thought it were just me. I did northern Italy last year by rail, every connection on its own tab, backup options in a different colour.
Tariq: Backup options in a different colour. That's the right way to do it.
Graham: Me daughter thinks I'm mad. I'm learning Italian an' all, four hundred and twelve days on Duolingo.
Tariq: That's commitment. I'm on an app for my written Urdu and I'm nowhere near four hundred days.
Graham: Get on with it then! You follow football? I'm a Forest man meself.
Tariq: No. Cricket. Pakistan, and Essex.
Graham: Cricket. Well, at least it's not rugby. I've just had a lady tell me she watches rugby.
Tariq: Pakistan will wind you up more than any football team, I promise you. They collapsed from a winning position last week. Again.
Graham: Ha, you want to try being Forest. We've had forty years of—
calls.C0402:
Gemma: Hiya! Graham, is it? I'm Gemma.
Graham: Hello, duck. Yes, Graham. Can you hear me alright?
Gemma: Yeah, perfect. I've got to say, when I saw your photo you reminded me of my dad. The canal painting and everything. He's always walking the canal.
Graham: Oh, I'll take that as a compliment, I think. Where are you?
Gemma: Walsall. I walk our dog along the canal most days, and round the Arboretum.
Graham: Walsall canal. Now that's a proper bit of history, that. All them branches round there used to be packed with boats for the foundries and the leather works.
Gemma: My dad worked in a leather factory! Then he drove a delivery van.
Graham: There you go. Me dad drove a lorry. And me mum was a dinner lady.
Gemma: No way, so was my mum! She's retired now, but the kids at the school still stop her in Asda.
Graham: Ha, mine were the same. Couldn't go anywhere. So what do you do, Gemma?
Gemma: Erm, I'm an assistant dog groomer, two days a week, and I'm doing a psychology degree with the Open University. Second year. I want to go into mental health, eventually, if I don't leave it too late.
Graham: Too late? How old are you, if you don't mind me asking?
Gemma: Thirty-five.
Graham: No, see, that's not late, that. I'm fifty-eight and I've just started watercolours and Italian. You've got thirty year of work in you yet. And I saw them course books in your picture. That's somebody who means it.
Gemma: Aw, that's really kind. I do worry I'm not clever enough sometimes. My marks are alright though.
Graham: Well then. Marks don't lie. What are you doing on it at the minute?
Gemma: Erm, a module on anxiety and how people cope with stress, which is sort of close to home, I had a bit of that in my twenties. Sorry, is that too much? I always say too much.
Graham: Not at all. I had a bad year meself before I packed in engineering. Stress, then me heart started going funny. So I know a bit about it from the wrong end. You'd be good at that job, I reckon. You're easy to talk to.
Gemma: That's two people who've said that today, I'm gonna get big-headed. Are you alright now, with your heart?
Graham: Oh, it's managed. Tablets, and I walk twenty thousand steps a day on the round. I'm a postie now. Get up at half four.
Gemma: Half four! I'd be useless. My dad won't even go the doctor's, he's terrible. I'm always on at him.
Graham: Keep on at him. Honestly. I left it far too long, I should've gone months before I did.
Gemma: I'll tell him a postman from Beeston said so. Do you follow football? My dad drags me to Walsall a couple of times a season.
Graham: Forest, all me life. Walsall, though, I'll give you credit for that, it takes a special kind of suffering.
Gemma: Ha! It does. We have a bacon bap at half time and that's the best bit.
Graham: A bap? It's a cob, duck.
Gemma: It's a bap! What's a cob?
Graham: It's a cob. Same thing, round, bread, bacon in it. Saturday morning, there's a new bakery on the High Road does a cracking—
calls.C0403:
Nicola: Hiya! Last one, isn't it? I'm Nicola.
Tariq: Tariq. Hi. Yeah, last one.
Nicola: How've you found it? I've had a lovely time, everyone's been so chatty.
Tariq: It's been fine. Better than I expected, honestly.
Nicola: Ha, what did you expect?
Tariq: Three minutes of talking about the weather. It's been more interesting than that.
Nicola: Well, I'll try not to mention the weather then. So what do you do, Tariq?
Tariq: Operations for a facilities management company in London. Cleaning, security, maintenance contracts for office buildings. You?
Nicola: I'm a dental hygienist, two days a week in Frome. In Somerset.
Tariq: Right. So you're the one who tells people off about flossing.
Nicola: No! I never tell anyone off. That's the whole trick, you chat them through it, you ask about their grandkids, and they don't even notice you're scraping away. It's sort of like being a hairdresser, only with more blood.
Tariq: That's a terrible selling point.
Nicola: Ha, yeah, don't put that on the leaflet. You drink a lot of coffee, I reckon. You've got the look.
Tariq: Sorry, what look is that exactly?
Nicola: I don't know, organised. Busy. Bit tired round the eyes. Sorry, that's rude!
Tariq: No, it's accurate. Three or four a day. I'm fussy about it, though, there's a new place by Stratford station that's actually decent.
Nicola: Well, I won't lecture you. Do you get away much, with a job like that?
Tariq: One proper trip a year. Japan was the last one. Before that Uzbekistan, Samarkand and Bukhara. And Andalusia, for the Alhambra.
Nicola: Oh, I've always wanted to see the Alhambra! I did Lisbon with my girlfriends. Was it worth it?
Tariq: Completely. Go early, book the Nasrid Palaces slot weeks ahead, and go to Córdoba as well, the Mezquita. People skip Córdoba and they shouldn't. It's about two hours on the train, there's a fast one from Granada now, and honestly the inside of the Mezquita, all those arches going on and on in the half-dark, it's one of the best buildings I've ever stood in.
Nicola: See, now I want to go. You'd be a proper good person to travel with, you'd know where everything was.
Tariq: I would. I'd also want to leave at seven in the morning.
Nicola: Ah, that's me out then. I'm more of a sit at the next table and make friends with the waiter sort of person. I'm going to New Zealand one day, that's my big one.
Tariq: One day meaning when?
Nicola: Erm, once Alfie's done his GCSEs and I've saved up. So, never, probably!
Tariq: Put a date on it. Then work back from the date. Otherwise it stays "one day".
Nicola: That's proper sensible. Annoyingly sensible. Do you do that with everything?
Tariq: Pretty much. My mum says I'd plan breakfast if she let me.
Nicola: Ha! I like your mum already. Has she got—

C0399.line_text: I do, yeah. Separated a couple of years. I've got two grown-up kids, son in Nottingham who I see most Sundays, and me daughter's up in Leeds. Don't see her as much as I'd like.
C0399.what: His voice catches and goes thick on 'me daughter's up in Leeds'. He pauses for about two seconds, swallows and glances down away from the camera before finishing the sentence more quietly.
